711.event_title: John F. Kennedy addresses the Greater Houston Ministerial Association
711.place: Rice Hotel, Houston, Texas, United States
711.event: During the 1960 presidential campaign, Senator John F. Kennedy spoke to the Greater Houston Ministerial Association, a gathering of clergy, at the Rice Hotel in Houston, to address concerns about his Catholic faith, noting that no Catholic had ever been elected president. He set out his support for religious tolerance and the absolute separation of church and state, said he was not the Catholic candidate for president but the Democratic Party's candidate who happened also to be a Catholic, and asked to be judged on his record of fourteen years in Congress. He then took questions from the ministers.
711.explanation: Kennedy chose his audience deliberately and spoke directly to the doubts that this particular assembly of clergy held about him.
711.tie_back: The kural asks speakers to understand the assembly in front of them before weighing their words, and Kennedy shaped his address precisely to the concerns of the ministers he faced.
711._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of reading an assembly before speaking, with the speech built around the hearers' specific worries.

712.event_title: Nehru's Tryst with Destiny speech at the midnight of independence
712.event: The Constituent Assembly of India met at eleven at night on 14 August 1947, and Jawaharlal Nehru moved a resolution that its members take a pledge of service to India after the last stroke of midnight. Introducing it, he said: At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom. As the clock struck twelve, the President and members stood and took the pledge.
712.explanation: Nehru timed his words to the exact moment of independence, so that the speech and the event it described became one.
712.tie_back: The kural tells good speakers to pick the right moment before they speak, and Nehru delivered his most famous words at the very hour they were meant for.
712._accuracy_note: A strong example of choosing the moment for speech, though the moment was set by the transfer of power rather than chosen by reading the audience's mood.

713.event_title: Wagner's Tannhauser is whistled off the stage of the Paris Opera
713.place: Paris Opera (Salle Le Peletier), Paris, France
713.event: Wagner revised Tannhauser for the Paris Opera and, to meet its convention, agreed to add a ballet, but he placed it in the first act rather than in its traditional place in the second. Members of the Jockey Club, who usually arrived after dinner for the second half of the evening and missed the dancing, disrupted the performances with whistles and catcalls, joined by political opponents of the production's sponsors. After 164 rehearsals, the opera was withdrawn after only three performances.
713.explanation: However strong the music, Wagner's disregard of what the Paris audience expected turned the premiere into a fiasco.
713.tie_back: The kural says one who speaks without first understanding the assembly shows no real ability, and Wagner's refusal to accommodate the Paris Opera's audience sank the production despite its merits.
713._accuracy_note: A strong case of misjudging an audience, though Wagner acted from artistic conviction rather than ignorance, and political hostility also played a part.

714.event_title: Faraday gives The Chemical History of a Candle to a young audience
714.place: Royal Institution, London, England, United Kingdom
714.event: The Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures for young people began in 1825, and Michael Faraday delivered nineteen series of them. His last, given when he was 70 in late December 1860 and early 1861, was a set of six lectures on The Chemical History of a Candle to an audience averaging about 650 young people, using a simple candle and many demonstrations to explain combustion. In the lectures he spoke of himself and his listeners together as fellow philosophers and even as fellow juveniles, and the lectures were published in 1861 and have never been out of print.
714.explanation: One of the greatest scientists of his day set aside the language of the laboratory and met children on their own ground, and the result became a classic.
714.tie_back: The kural advises speakers to shine fully among the learned but to take on a plain colour before those without learning, and Faraday wrapped deep science in the plain language of a candle for his young hearers.
714._accuracy_note: A strong fit for adapting to a less learned audience, though Faraday simplified rather than concealed his learning, and his hearers were children rather than fools.

715.event_title: Thomas Jefferson's silence in the Continental Congress
715.event: Thomas Jefferson, a young Virginia delegate in the Continental Congress, rarely spoke in its debates, and John Adams later recalled that during the whole time he sat with him in Congress he never heard him utter three sentences together. Jefferson was nonetheless known for a masterly pen, and in June 1776 he was named to the committee to prepare the Declaration of Independence alongside Adams, the elder Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman and Robert Livingston, which entrusted him with the draft. Adams reflected in his autobiography that eloquence in public assemblies was not the surest road to fame, pointing to the reserve of Washington, Franklin and Jefferson.
715.explanation: Jefferson let senior and more forceful members carry the floor, and his restraint left him trusted with the most important writing of all.
715.tie_back: The kural praises the restraint that does not rush to speak first among wiser elders, and Jefferson's quiet in Congress earned him the confidence of his seniors.
715._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit, since Jefferson's silence reflected his temperament and dislike of debate as much as deference to elders.

716.event_title: Benjamin Disraeli's maiden speech is shouted down in the House of Commons
716.place: House of Commons, London, England, United Kingdom
716.event: Benjamin Disraeli, elected for Maidstone in 1837, was already ridiculed for his dandified appearance and affected manner when he rose to make his first speech in the House of Commons. Members heckled and mocked him, and he defiantly declared as he sat down that the time would come when they would hear him. He went on to become a celebrated parliamentary debater and, in 1868 and again from 1874, prime minister.
716.explanation: Before the most demanding audience in the country, a gifted speaker's misjudged first appearance turned into a famous humiliation that took him years to overcome.
716.tie_back: The kural compares a slip in speech before learned and experienced people to losing one's footing on the path, and Disraeli's maiden speech was just such a fall before the Commons.
716._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a slip before a demanding audience, though the hostility Disraeli faced had political as well as rhetorical causes.

717.event_title: Hilbert and Klein bring Emmy Noether to Gottingen
717.event: In 1915 the leading Gottingen mathematicians David Hilbert and Felix Klein invited Emmy Noether, then working without pay at Erlangen, to help with mathematical problems connected with the theory of relativity, because they needed an expert in invariant theory. She soon proved the result now called Noether's theorem, linking symmetries in physics to conservation laws, which Einstein praised for its penetrating mathematical thinking. Because women could not then obtain the habilitation, her courses were advertised under Hilbert's name while he and Klein fought the university authorities, and in 1919 she was finally made a Privatdozent.
717.explanation: Noether's brilliance, long unrecognised in its official standing, was recognised and championed by the very people best able to judge it.
717.tie_back: The kural says real learning shines among those who can judge words flawlessly, and Noether's genius found its proper setting among the greatest mathematicians of Gottingen.
717._accuracy_note: A strong fit for learning recognised by expert judges, though sources differ slightly on whether she arrived in 1915 or 1916.

718.event_title: Einstein translates and extends Satyendra Nath Bose's paper
718.place: Dacca (now Dhaka, Bangladesh) and Berlin, Germany
718.event: In 1924 Satyendra Nath Bose, a physicist at Dacca University, wrote a short paper deriving Planck's radiation law without relying on classical physics; he sent it to Philosophical Magazine but heard nothing back. He then sent it to Albert Einstein, who received it in June 1924, recognised that it solved a problem he had struggled with, translated it into German himself and had it published in Zeitschrift fur Physik in August 1924. Einstein quickly extended Bose's method to material particles, leading to what became known as Bose-Einstein statistics and the prediction of Bose-Einstein condensation.
718.explanation: Bose's ideas, ignored by one journal, bore fruit almost at once when they reached a mind ready to understand and develop them.
718.tie_back: The kural likens speaking to people of understanding to watering a garden bed where the plants are already growing, and Bose's work flourished the moment it reached Einstein.
718._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural, with the same paper meeting silence in one place and immediate growth in the hands of a receptive expert.

719.event_title: Pablo Casals refuses to perform in countries that recognised Franco's regime
719.event: The Catalan cellist Pablo Casals, an outspoken opponent of fascism, settled in Prades in French Catalonia and refused to return to Spain after the Spanish Civil War. In 1946 he announced his retirement from public performance in protest at worldwide recognition of the Franco regime, extending his boycott to countries such as the United States and the United Kingdom that maintained relations with Spain. He resumed public performance in 1950 only in Prades, where the Casals Festival was founded, and later made rare exceptions such as his 1961 performance at the White House for President Kennedy.
719.explanation: One of the world's greatest musicians withheld his art from stages he considered compromised, offering it only where it could serve his convictions.
719.tie_back: The kural says those who can speak good things well in a worthy assembly should never offer them in an unworthy one, and Casals kept his music back from audiences he would not dignify with it.
719._accuracy_note: A next-best fit: Casals's boycott was a political protest against governments rather than a judgement on the quality of particular audiences.

720.event_title: Mendel's laws of heredity are presented in Brunn and then overlooked
720.event: After years of experiments crossing garden peas, the Augustinian monk Gregor Mendel presented his results on the inheritance of traits to the Brunn Natural Science Society in 1865, and they were published in 1866 in the society's relatively obscure proceedings. The work, which laid the mathematical foundation of genetics, remained largely overlooked during his lifetime. It was rediscovered around 1900 by Carl Correns, Hugo de Vries and Erich Tschermak, some fifteen years after Mendel's death.
720.explanation: One of the most important discoveries in biology was offered to listeners and readers who did not grasp its value, and it lay unused for a generation.
720.tie_back: The kural compares speaking before those who cannot share one's understanding to nectar spilled into a gutter, not spoiled but wasted, much as Mendel's insight lay unused for thirty-five years.
720._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for wisdom wasted on an unready audience, though historians debate how fully Mendel was ignored and the Brunn society was not an unworthy assembly.
